  4. Require opt-in before a detected formatter runs on save … 

    Since 66c9fd65 formatOnSave defaulted to true whenever a formatCommand
was in play, including one the FormatterRegistry auto-detected from

and upstream, where nothing touches a file at save time unless the
user installed a bundle that asks to.

  8. Offer Run in Terminal where the command is written … 

    Until now runLocation could only be set by editing a bundle item's
plist by hand, which made the whole feature invisible to anyone working
in the Bundle Editor. Both panes that own a command now carry the check
box: regular commands and drag commands alike, since a drop handler
runs down the same path.

The pane also has to say what checking it costs. A terminal command
owns a pty, so everything on the input/output axis is inert for it —
the regular pane greys those controls out while the box is checked, and
both panes name, underneath, whatever the item asked for that will not
be honoured. command::ignored_settings answers that question by
comparing parsed values against the defaults for the kind of item,
because key presence would be useless: the editor materialises input,
outputLocation and their neighbours into every command it opens, so
every terminal command would look like a conflict. Drag commands parse
with defaults of their own, which is why the caller says which kind it
holds.

The warning is spelled in plist keys rather than in the labels above
it, because half of what it can report — fallbackInput, outputReuse,
autoRefresh — has no control in either pane and can only have arrived
by hand; those keys join BindingKeys so the pane notices them changing
under it. And the value transformer shields the binding machinery from
an item whose runLocation is not a string at all, showing such an item
as the default instead of refusing to open it.

  9. Gather the terminal launchers under the Terminal menu … 

    A runLocation:terminal command already appears in the Bundles menu and
⌃⌘T like any other, with its key equivalent and scope filtering. What
it has no place in is the menu named after the thing it does: the
Terminal menu starts a shell and two agent CLIs and then stops, so
"start something in a terminal" is the one phrasing of the feature the
menus never answer.

The class that opts a command in is terminal.launcher — deliberately
not under callback., which is for events TextMate fires, and this is
not one. It matches by prefix, so terminal.launcher.rails answers too,
the same way callback.document.will-save does.

Two decisions the selection turns on. It asks bundles::query not to
filter by scope rank, because the default keeps only the best match and
one launcher scoped to the current language would otherwise take the
whole menu with it. And it re-reads runLocation from the parsed command
rather than trusting the class, so a command that declares itself a
launcher but still runs in-process cannot advertise a terminal tab that
never opens.

Answered by AppController rather than the window controller so the menu
is populated with no window open — the context the application-level
route exists for, where picking a launcher opens the window it needs.

  10. Hand a command to the terminal instead of forking it … 

    The execution route for runLocation:terminal. OakCommand recognises the
key before any of its fork-and-collect machinery starts, writes the
script under its readable name and asks its delegate for a terminal
instead; OakCommandTerminalUnavailableError names the one way that can
fail. The document window answers by opening a terminal tab whose
session starts from the command's own composed environment — document
and project variables included — rather than from the window's.

What the window layers underneath is
TerminalEnvironmentByAddingExtras: mate on PATH, TM_AGENT_BRIDGE for
any harness that can register an MCP server and wants TextMate's
editor context, and the Claude IDE-context variables while the bridge
runs. Every terminal TextMate spawns is expected to carry these,
because after the script exits the tab lives on as an ordinary
interactive shell. The base wins — integration variables are inserted
only when absent, and the TM_MATE directory joins PATH at lower
precedence than anything the command brought — and the helper is
idempotent, so it can run before requiredCommands is checked and again
at the window with no drift.

A command invoked with no document window — the Bundles menu at
application level — gets the window it needed: AppController creates an
untitled window and forwards the same hand-off to it, with the user's
home as the working directory that window's own terminal would have
opened in anyway. Falling back to an in-process run would keep whatever
outputLocation the command was left at, and could paste a dev server's
stdout into a document. oak::application_t's path globals sit behind a
mutex now, because this route asks for them off the main thread.

    Kazuhiro Sakai authored August 3, 2026

  11. Let a command say where it runs, not just where output goes … 

    A command that starts something interactive — a dev server, a REPL, an
agent — has nothing to say through outputLocation: every value on that
axis assumes TextMate forked the script, fed it stdin and collected its
output. runLocation is the orthogonal key: "editor" is today's
behaviour and the default, "terminal" means the command owns a pty and
TextMate neither feeds it input nor sees what it prints.

This is the command-framework half. The parser carries the key, and
create_named_script_path gives a script the user will see on their own
command line a readable "«name»-«sha1»" cache entry instead of the bare
digest — sanitised so a name cannot start with a dot, and working where
there is no app bundle to name the cache directory after.

Import/export filters refuse terminal commands: the filter runner forks
the script and reads back its output, so treating a terminal command as
a filter would run it with a document on its stdin. Eligibility is
settled before the scope-rank cutoff, not after — bundles::query keeps
only the best-ranked matches, so a narrowly scoped terminal command
would otherwise carry the cutoff away with it and hide the broadly
scoped filter that should have been chosen.

Pinning the runner's promises down in tests flushed out two waits that
were wrong from the start. wait_for_command could block forever when
the group's notification landed before CFRunLoopRun entered — a
CFRunLoopStop with nothing to stop. And waiting on the dispatch group
at all waits on the wrong thing: run_command posts the completion to
this run loop and only then leaves the group, so an empty group still
means did_exit has not run. It now waits on _process_id, the condition
wait() next door has always used.

  1. Give one bundle's opt-in the immediacy a tap's already had … 

    The Auto-Update column put both kinds of source in one place, and there
they answered differently: checking a tap applied what was waiting,
checking a repository subscribed to on its own only promised something
about the next scheduled wake. The argument for the tap's immediacy —
that a checkbox which changes nothing you can see reads as a broken one
— never depended on the kind of row, so the per-bundle setter now has
the same shape: save first, then a non-enqueuing poll of that one
subscription, inside the operation that saved it.

It lives in the setting's shared commit point rather than in the setter,
as a parameter, so there is still one place that changes a subscription,
saves, and puts the change back when the save does not land — and one
place that knows the poll may only run once it did land. Both UI entry
points get it: the sources row and the bundles-table menu. That does
change what *Update Automatically* means — it now accepts the update
already waiting rather than only future ones — which is why Compare sits
next to it for anyone who wants to read the diff first.

Also: a tap with neither a name nor a URL, which takes a hand-edited
registry, no longer gets called ‘(null)’ in the tooltip that names it.

  2. Let a tap be trusted instead of each of its bundles … 

    Auto-update is opt-in per bundle, which is right for a repository
subscribed to on its own but means twenty right-clicks for a tap the
user curates themselves — twenty gestures all saying one sentence, "I
trust this source". A tap now carries that sentence as a setting of its
own: off by default, like the per-bundle flag it never touches.

The effective policy becomes the OR of the two, computed rather than
stored, so checking the box rewrites no subscription records and
unchecking it gives back exactly the state that was there before. Trust
covers what the tap actually vouches for and no more: a ref the user
chose, a bundle dropped from the catalogue, and a tap that is no longer
registered all fall back to the per-bundle flag. A catalogue that moved
a bundle to a different repository still blocks the apply outright — a
compromised tap must not be able to redirect a subscription and have the
new source installed.

Enabling trust polls that tap's subscriptions on the spot, inside the
setter's own queued operation: checking a box and watching a row sit at
"update available" until the next daily wake would read as the box not
having worked, and going through the public poll entry point would
enqueue behind the operation waiting for it.

The pane says the same thing in three places. Sources get an
Auto-Update checkbox column — one column, one meaning, for taps and
one-off repositories alike. A bundle whose tap owns the setting shows
it checked and disabled, with a tooltip naming the tap; one whose source
moved shows it disabled too, with the reason it is paused. And the
global checkbox no longer promises to install everything below it: it
now says it installs the trusted ones.

  5. Give the bookmark column back … 

    Diagnostics arrived in this fork as marks in the bookmark column, with
the message as their payload — which made the popover behind a click
the only way to read one, and made a column that already had a job mean
two things. Every part of that role now has a surface of its own: the
squiggle says where, hover and dwell say what, the pane surveys the
workspace, the minimap lane locates within the file, and the status bar
counts. So the publisher stops writing to the gutter, and a click on a
line a server has complained about is a bookmark again.

The two features that read those marks back as data move to the buffer
with them. Whether the cursor's line has a problem — what decides a
code-action probe — is a line query whose end is inclusive, because a
point diagnostic on an empty line sits on exactly the one index a
half-open window would skip. Next/Previous Diagnostic runs off the
buffer's own sorted index of reported positions rather than the
diagnostic list: a zero-length diagnostic at end of line borrows the
previous character to draw its squiggle, and navigation must land the
caret where the server pointed — for a missing semicolon, one past the
borrowed character — so the growth direction is kept and the reported
positions are deduplicated into single stops. The offer is made on what
the buffer can navigate to, not on what the store counted, since a jump
that silently does nothing reads as the whole feature being broken.
This takes the last caller of nextMarkOfTypes:/prevMarkOfTypes:, both
fork additions for that one caller, with it.

What stays is the generic path the marks travelled on: `mate --set-mark
'error:message' --line N` predates the fork and is how a bundle points
at the line its build or lint step objected to. Publishing used to
clear all three mark types on arrival, taking a bundle's marks down
with it; it no longer touches them. The regression test publishes
through the manager operation the marks were written from — restoring
the deleted publish body fails it on the first assertion.

  6. Give the minimap's other edge to diagnostics … 

    The minimap already carries SCM diff at its left edge and is the only
per-file overview the editor has. Diagnostics take the right edge —
the overview-ruler convention — drawn as an overlay so no content inset
moves. The lane gets no row tint of its own: two translucent colours
blended over one row is where the two systems would actually collide,
while two strips at opposite edges are unambiguous by position. The
data is the buffer's diagnostics, not the gutter's marks, so the lane
shifts with the text between publishes and outlives the gutter's
diagnostic presentation.

The two rules a lane needs — which rows a range covers, which rows a
publish invalidates — live in a model free of AppKit, directly
testable. Every line a multi-line range crosses is marked and the worst
severity wins; the query takes a line window so drawing a dirty rect
costs a lookup over that rect, not a walk of the document. Markers are
four by four — wider than the diff strip because they draw over the
code blocks, two rows tall so a single-line diagnostic is not a speck —
centred on their row, drawn worst-last so an error survives a note on
the next line. Rows are invalidated in exactly one place, which applies
the marker's overhang itself; the caller repainting a caret line should
not have to know how far past its row a marker reaches. The strip cache
is keyed by the palette colour, so the map from severity to colour
exists only in ct::diagnostic_color.

Under this, the extent a publish reports becomes half-open for points
too: [p, p) reported as [p, p] fell outside its own extent whenever p
was a row start — exactly where the bridge puts every point it makes —
so a publish that moved a point diagnostic left its marker on screen
until an unrelated repaint passed by. Reporting [p, p + 1) fixes it
where the ambiguity is rather than teaching each consumer to guess: the
text view's clamp allows one past the end of the buffer, the minimap
drops the generosity it only needed under the old contract, and tests
pin the distinction at EOF — a range stopping there leaves the empty
last line alone, a point on it does not. The repaint path itself is
covered by a test driving a real OakTextView through a runtime-built
subclass recording setNeedsDisplayInRect:, since reverting the clamp
was otherwise invisible to the suite. Comments arguing from the old
extent are gone with it.

Investigated in DIAGNOSTICS_POINT_INVALIDATION_FINDINGS.md.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

    Kazuhiro Sakai authored July 31, 2026

  7. Survey every problem the servers reported in one pane … 

    Squiggles, hover and dwell all answer "what is wrong here" — none of
them answers "what is wrong at all". A workspace server analyses far
more than the file on screen, and until now the only way to see any of
it was to open every file and look.

The foundation is ownership. Diagnostics move out of a manager-global
URI map into LSPDiagnosticsStore, keyed by the publishing client and
then by URI — by client *identity*, not the workspace-root-plus-command
key, because a restart puts a new client under the same composite key
and the dying process must not take its successor's diagnostics with
it. Closing an editor keeps the entry, since the client is still
responsible for the file; terminate, restart and stop purge everything
the departing client published, URI-driven so an open document a dead
client published for but did not own is brought back in line; a publish
from a client the manager has already let go is ignored, so one parsed
just before Stop Server cannot resurrect a dead server's diagnostics.
shutdownAll purges explicitly — it cannot lean on the termination
callback, whose weak reference dies with the client. Workspace scoping
is containment both ways, symlinks resolved on both sides.

The pane itself hosts the way the diff pane does and the two are peers.
Rows group by file, sorted by path then position, with per-file and
window-wide counts describing what is actually listed under them. An
NSOutlineView recycles rows, publishes coalesce through one
main-run-loop hop, and a per-workspace revision — versions per client,
so a server publishing in another project cannot invalidate this one —
lets an idle project's re-publishes stop at a comparison instead of
rebuilding the list. When the list does rebuild, the scroll position is
restored and the selection re-found by what it names; collapse state
survives rebuilds but expires with the file going clean.

Clicking a row focuses or opens the tab — found by inode, not by how
the server spelled the path — waits for the load, and only then
converts the UTF-16 column. The tab bar moves with the editor when a
background tab is selected, the load a row starts is balanced exactly
once (on failure OakDocument has already closed itself), and a
cross-file row neither steals first responder nor spares the disposable
tab. The empty pane says "No diagnostics reported." — completeness is
the server's to promise, not the pane's.

The severity palette moves into ct::diagnostic_color, read by both the
squiggle and the panel's dots: a dot and the squiggle under the same
text have to be the same red or the two stop reading as one system.

  8. Read a diagnostic at the caret or under the pointer … 

    Seeing a squiggle is not reading the message, and the only way to read
one was to click the gutter mark. Two surfaces replace that.

The hover command (⌃⌘H) prepends a diagnostics section to its tooltip.
Diagnostics are known locally, so when a server round-trip is needed
the section shows immediately and is re-shown combined when the
response arrives; the async completion re-reads the buffer instead of
reusing a stale capture, and a re-publish rebuilds the local half in
place while the server's sections stay put. Pointing at a squiggle
shows its message after a 0.35 s dwell, reusing the tracking area the
⌘-definition cursor already installs; the mouse-moved path asks the
buffer for the range containing the pointer, so pointer motion stays
O(log n) per severity.

Command and dwell share one tooltip, so it has an owner and a
generation: dwell taking over cancels the outstanding request, a late
hover completion presents nothing if its generation is stale, and dwell
stands down when a ⌃⌘H tooltip is already open at the same index rather
than downgrading it to diagnostics-only content. The fire path
re-checks the situation it was armed for — the pointer can leave the
view directly from a squiggle, and a click that dismissed the popover
must not have it dragged straight back. Selected-tab state moves out of
the SwiftUI view into an observable owned by the tooltip, keyed by
section label, so re-presenting updated content does not pull the
reader back to the first tab.

Diagnostics a terminated server can no longer retract are cleared
through the same path a grammar switch uses, and an empty publish
removes the cache entry rather than storing an emptied one — a clean
file is the absence of a diagnostic. A test pins what an edit does to a
point diagnostic: it is relocated onto the edit boundary rather than
dropped, an asymmetry that was deliberate but until now
indistinguishable from an oversight.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
    c0cc52dbcc Browse code
    Kazuhiro Sakai authored July 31, 2026

  9. Store diagnostics in the buffer and draw them as squiggles … 

    A server re-analyzes roughly 300 ms after a keystroke, so between an
edit and the next publishDiagnostics the reported coordinates describe
text that is no longer there. Keeping the diagnostics in the buffer
means the ranges shift with the edit and stay attached to the code they
annotate.

Storage is one sorted list of diagnostic_t — range, normalized severity
and the message/source/code payload — plus two indexes derived from it:
per-severity coalesced ranges for drawing and hit testing, and a list
of zero-width points. The list is the source of truth on purpose:
because the payload travels with the range, a squiggle and the message
read at the same index cannot end up in different coordinate systems.
replace() applies an edit the way the buffer performs it, deletion then
insertion, which is what makes an edit aligned with an endpoint behave
like an insertion there. set() reports both whether the drawn extent
moved and whether the set differs at all, since a re-publish can change
a message without moving anything.

-[OakDocument setDiagnostics:] converts the LSP dictionary shape into
buffer ranges. LSP columns are UTF-16 code units, so they are advanced
through the line's own text; out-of-range positions clamp, reversed
ranges are dropped. An empty range — a missing token — grows onto the
next character on its line, else the previous one, records that it did,
and hit-tests end-inclusively so a caret at end of line still reads
"expected ';'". The severity class every surface agrees on is
normalized here: 1 error, 2 warning, everything else note.

Squiggles draw severities 3 → 1 so an error lands on top of a warning
it overlaps, are not suppressed under the selection, and align the
wave's phase to absolute x so a diagnostic spanning several style runs
draws as one continuous line. A zero-width point is drawn by
paragraph_t itself, since its position may have no glyph run at all.
Diagnostics get their own invalidation entry point instead of borrowing
did_update_scopes: they change no layout and no scopes, so affected
rows need only a repaint.

Application runs on arrival, on open and on reload — a workspace server
analyzes files ahead of the user opening them and will not republish
when nothing changed, and reloading swaps out the buffer content the
ranges were stored in.

arrangement we were trying to get out of.

system ruby, else a clear failure. Nothing is searched for beyond that, which is
what the shim it grew out of already decided. The day Apple removes the system

TM_RUBY naming one of our own shims is refused rather than obeyed. It would exec
in a circle — shim to resolver to shim, forever, without so much as spawning a
process to notice. And it is a plausible thing to find: `ruby18` chose a real
interpreter for years, so it can sit in a .tm_properties from when it meant one,
and the Ruby bundle reads TM_RUBY as a bare command name, which is exactly the
spelling that loops.

name in the shebang and what bundle items written against it may already
require, so each shim passes its own answer and ruby18 passes the off it has had
since it stopped downloading its own interpreter — most of the reason a command
starts in 20 ms rather than 80.

someone's own ruby install reached bundle items through the command environment,
where it breaks them in ways that are near impossible to see from inside a

on the grounds that whoever names an interpreter meant the one they configured.

  2. Treat bundles shipped in the app as built-in … 

    BundlesManager and the bundle loader do not know about each other. Now that a
bundle inside the app outranks the Managed copy of the same UUID, that gap
shows: BundlesManager keeps downloading and updating a Bundle Support in
Managed that the loader eclipses every time, and Preferences reports the
version and date of a copy no command ever runs.

Give Bundle an explicit builtIn state, read from the info.plist UUIDs in
Contents/SharedSupport/Bundles. Identity comes from what is inside the app
right now, not from the local index or from a path, so no copy elsewhere can
claim it.

A built-in bundle is installed by virtue of being in the app, whatever the
index says and whether or not a Managed copy is still on disk. It has no
update to offer, because the dates the index publishes describe that eclipsed
copy. It is excluded from the auto-update predicate — stated there rather than
left to follow from the other terms, since it is mandatory and that is exactly
the kind of thing an edit here would quietly undo.

The ‘Updated’ column asks when the source last changed this bundle, so for a
built-in it answers with the application: the index date belongs to the copy
that is not running, and the files inside the app carry whatever modification
dates they had when they were imported, which for Bundle Support is 2023 and
says nothing about which version this is. The build date is what a built-in
bundle is versioned with. Only the download date is replaced — lastUpdated
still describes the Managed copy, and is what reaches the local index.

The refusal is at the model boundary, not only in the UI: installBundles: (after
the dependency walk, so it cannot arrive as somebody else's requirement),
uninstallBundle:, and markBundleUninstalled: all decline. That covers the paths
the Bundles pane does not own — dependency installation, and restoring an
official bundle when a subscription is removed.

The in-app path is never written to Bundle.path, so it cannot reach the local
index; path keeps describing the Managed copy, which is left alone. It is only
eclipsed, and with the predicate exclusion in place it stays gone if the user
deletes it.

  3. Take the bundle support library off Rosetta … 

    Three things in Bundle Support only work under ruby 1.8.7, and the only 1.8.7
we have is a 2012 x86_64 build downloaded from archive.textmate.org. That build
runs under Rosetta 2, which is being phased out, and it is what 312 commands
across 43 bundles are pinned to.

lib/osx/plist.bundle was the load-bearing one: a CoreFoundation C extension
last built for ppc/i386/x86_64, so it cannot load in an arm64 ruby, and
textmate.rb requires it. That reaches much further than property lists — the
tm_dialog v1 protocol is plists over stdin/stdout, so it reaches every command
that opens a nib dialog. Replace it with lib/osx/plist.rb. require resolves .rb
ahead of .bundle, so no caller changes: not the 312 commands, not the ten
bundles using OSX::PropertyList.

Reading goes through the pure-ruby plist gem already vendored here, after
plutil(1) normalises binary and OpenStep input to XML — binary is what
.tmCommand files actually are. Writing does not go through the gem: its
generator re-indents every line of what it is handed, including newlines inside
a string value, so a command body would gain a tab per nesting level on each
round trip. 1,211 of 2,318 real bundle plists came back different. The shim
emits what CoreFoundation emitted instead, byte for byte — keys in UTF-16
code-unit order, which is CF's and stops agreeing with byte order at U+10000 —
and every public entry point (to_plist, Plist::Emit.dump, both shapes of
OSX::PropertyList.dump) reaches this emitter, so no door is left open onto the
gem's.

The boundaries the corpus cannot measure are pinned by tests instead: the
installed bundles hold no NaN, no out-of-range integer, no non-UTF-8 string
and no DateTime. NaN and the infinities use the spellings CoreFoundation wrote
and plutil still normalises to, in both directions — the gem read them all as
0.0 without a word. Integers are refused outside signed 64-bit: plutil lints
wider values happily, but CoreFoundation reads an <integer> as
kCFNumberSInt64Type and wraps — TextMate's own reader included — and a file
that lints clean but reads back as a different number is worse than a refusal.
Strings that cannot be represented as UTF-8 are refused rather than written
into a document that declares UTF-8, where one stray byte costs the whole file.
DateTime is converted to UTC before Date, which it subclasses, gets to stamp a
Z on a wall clock. The tests use a hand-rolled harness rather than test/unit or
minitest: both are gems, and bundle commands run with --disable-gems, so a test
needing rubygems would not be testing the environment the shim runs in.

bin/ruby18 is kept, not deleted. $TM_SUPPORT_PATH/bin is on PATH, so deleting
it would stop 43 bundles the moment it shipped; and a shim reaches bundles we
do not ship, which a shebang rewrite never could. It now execs the system ruby
and refuses to download an interpreter — private/ruby18_fix_loadpath.rb, which
existed to patch the downloaded build's baked-in paths, goes with that. The
version guard is loaded with -r as an absolute path, expanded without a
subshell: ruby looks a relative -r up in the load path rather than the working
directory, and this is on the path of every ruby18 command. --disable-gems
lives in the shim rather than in 312 shebangs: rubygems is most of a bare
ruby's startup, and with it disabled this is faster than the Rosetta 1.8.7 it
replaces.

lib/shelltokenize.rb had a regexp literal with \x7F-\xFF in it, which has been
a SyntaxError since 1.9 and made the file unloadable. Its byte offsets were
also being used to slice by character.

Checked against the C extension over every plist in the installed bundles —
2,318 files, parsed, emitted, and round-tripped under both implementations,
with no difference on real bundle data. The system ruby is Apple-deprecated
and this is a bridge, not a destination: phase 3 of the plan points ruby18,
ruby20 and plain ruby at a runtime the app ships itself.

    The shared library every bundle command loads — textmate.rb, ui.rb, the

downloaded from the index. That splits ownership in an unhelpful way: the app
ships one version and the support code it depends on is whatever the index
last handed out, here a 2023 copy. It also leaves nowhere durable to put a fix,
since anything written into Managed/ is replaced on the next bundle update.

last, which meant a bundle we ship could never be seen while a copy of the same
UUID sat in Managed — and Bundle Support is mandatory, so the index reinstalls

into the app now wins over anything an index or a subscription distributes,
while the user's local edits still win over us. TM_SUPPORT_PATH needs no change
— it expands from $TM_BUNDLE_SUPPORT of whichever copy actually loaded.

  7. Exclude outward-grown panes from the new-window frame … 

    Showing the Markdown preview (or the terminal pane) grows the window
outward, but -windowFrame — the basis for Cmd-N's cascaded frame and
the saved default frame — only subtracted the file browser width. A new
window therefore inherited the pane-inflated size despite opening with
no panes, and re-opening the preview there grew it even further.

Factor the preview's grow/shrink math into
-windowFrame:adjustedForMarkdownPreviewPaneVisible: (the terminal
pane's existing pattern) and have -windowFrame apply both panes' hide
math. The session snapshot is unaffected: it reads self.window.frame
directly, and the preview restores as visible with its frame intact.

  1. Stop following a symlink that leads back to itself … 

    A bundle directory is scanned through plist::cache_t, and three of its walks
follow symlinks with nothing to stop them: resolved() chases the chain, the
watch list does the same through copy_links(), and cleanup() decides
reachability through copy_all(). A link pointing at its own name — one mistyped
‘ln -s’ in ~/Library/Application Support/TextMate/Bundles — sends all three
round forever, and the first of them runs while the bundle index is built at
launch. The result is a segmentation fault before the first window, on every
launch, until the link is found and removed.

All three now give up after 32 links, the ceiling POSIX puts on the same
problem, and a chain that does not end is left as the link it is: no content,
no entries, so what it pointed at is simply absent. Everything else in the
directory still loads.

The tests build the two shapes that occur in practice — a link to itself and a
pair pointing at each other — and check the scan, the watch list, and cleanup.
Without the guards each of them takes the test binary down with a stack
overflow.

  5. Add bundle subscriptions: GitHub repositories and tap catalogues … 

    Subscribed bundles get their own install root and their own state file,
and the signed api.textmate.org path is left exactly as it was: its
index, signatures, LocalIndex.plist, and orphan reconciliation never see
a subscription. Adding "Subscribed" to bundles::locations() after
"Managed" is what makes the editor pick them up — the existing FS
watcher and index rebuild come along for free — and the order is
deliberate, since first location wins a UUID collision and an officially
signed bundle should always win it. Displacing a signed bundle is
instead an explicit, journalled Replace with the symmetric Restore on
unsubscribe, and mandatory bundles are refused outright.

A tap is one repository whose Taps/bundles.plist lists many bundles —
the Homebrew shape, and the unit the feature leads with, since GitHub
offers nothing better than an explicit curated list. Catalogue identity
is deliberately not bundle identity: an installed bundle is a UUID, a
candidate is (tap, UUID), so two taps may offer two forks of the same
bundle without either vanishing. Each validated catalogue is cached
immutably under the revision it came from, so taps and update offers
survive restart and offline.

The engine resolves a ref to a SHA through the ref advertisement,
extracts into a transaction directory, validates the info.plist UUID
there, and treats the registry write as the commit point throughout:
memory never holds a change the state file does not, a failed write puts
the change back, and every destructive boundary — install, update,
uninstall, Replace, Restore — is journalled and recovered at launch
before the first bundle index is built. A registry written by a newer
version, or one that cannot be read at all, loads read-only and refuses
every mutation. A repository whose root is not a bundle may still hold
several: each becomes its own subscription, updated together, removable
apart.

Pinned is the default — autoUpdate is the only bit that says otherwise —
and the daily poll still resolves every subscription's effective ref so
an update can be offered without being applied. One session fetches from
github.com, codeload, raw.githubusercontent.com, and api.github.com and
refuses any redirect that leaves those hosts; nothing on a timer touches
the metered REST API. Owner enumeration, the one feature that does, runs
only on explicit user action and follows pagination to the end.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
    a372fb05cb Browse code
    Kazuhiro Sakai authored July 26, 2026

  6. Add the GitHub URL and git ref advertisement parsers … 

    Bundle subscriptions resolve a branch, tag, or revision to a SHA before
fetching anything, and they do it through git's smart-HTTP ref
advertisement rather than api.github.com: the REST API allows 60
unauthenticated requests an hour, which a handful of subscriptions would
exhaust on a single poll, while the git protocol is unmetered.

Both parsers are pure and network-free, which is the whole reason they
are separate from the manager that will use them. The pkt-line reader
refuses malformed framing outright rather than returning what it managed
to read, and an annotated tag resolves to its peeled commit — the
revision a checkout of that tag would actually produce. It also reads
the HEAD symref, so an omitted ref can mean "the repository's default
branch" instead of a guessed 'main'.

The URL parser is the other half of the trust model: without a
signature, the github.com allow-list is part of what stands in for one,
so there is no way to construct a repository that points elsewhere.
Userinfo spellings, path traversal, dot-led names, and the host typed as
an owner are all refused. Owner URLs and the REST pagination Link header
are parsed here too, for the one user-initiated feature that does use
the REST API.

This registers the BundlesManager test target; the parsers are the
highest-value fixture tests in the change.

    The completion popup and hover tooltip render code that is syntax

carried a font, so its colors stayed at .textBackgroundColor and

drops a line's leading whitespace when the line does not fit the width
it is laid out in, which is most lines of real source at the 260pt doc
panel width. Carry the indentation as a paragraph indent instead, so it
survives wrapping and continuation lines align under the code. Copilot
suggestions start at column 0 of the caret line, so dedent them for

  4. Add native Codex IDE context bridge … 

    TextMate implements Codex TUI's version-0 IDE-context IPC natively, so
/ide works in Codex the way it does in editors Codex ships support for:
the app joins the user-level router at ~/.codex/ipc/ipc.sock as an IDE
client, and also owns a private TMPDIR fallback socket that
TextMate-launched Codex sessions inherit for when no router is running.
Discovery answers only for workspace roots inside an open project;
responses carry the active file, selection, and open tabs.

The wire format was observed against Codex CLI 0.145.0 on macOS — a
private protocol, not a published compatibility contract — so the JSON
envelope adapter is isolated in codex_ide_protocol.h and unit-tested as
the single update point for a future Codex change. macOS /var, /tmp, and
/etc aliases are normalized for workspace routing, socket permissions are
constrained (0700 directory, 0600 socket), and fd ownership is preserved
across shutdown and reconnect races.

With two native IDE routes in the tree, the Claude-only symbols are named
for their owner (ClaudeIDEContextServer, ClaudeIDEContextLockFile) while
AgentBridge remains the shared coordinator for Claude, Codex, and the MCP
shim; user-default storage keys and tm_agent wire commands are unchanged,
and the AI preferences pane splits into per-provider sections under one
Editor Context switch.

Hardening from review: each TextMate process joins the router under a
distinct textmate-<pid> client id so debug and production instances can
coexist, reconnects use exponential backoff (1s to 30s), IPC frames are
capped at 16 MiB, parent-of-project workspace roots are rejected as
ambiguous instead of answering with another project's context, and the
Codex response shares the 64 KiB selection cap with the Claude/MCP routes
so a whole-file selection cannot overflow a frame and vanish.

Squash of the 4-commit codex/experiment-codex-ide-context work,
review-closed and live-verified against Codex CLI 0.145.0.

app quit cannot kill the shim, tool replies are written off the main
thread so a stopped reader cannot freeze the editor, MCP protocol-version
negotiation echoes a known revision and otherwise answers with the newest

actually carry the data.

Jul 15, 2026

  1. Make symbol list extraction robust against parse batching … 

    Symbols are computed per did_parse() range, which for async parsing is
a batch of roughly ten lines (one line via wait_for_repair), so a
symbol whose scope run spans batches was flushed as a fragment at every
boundary. Bundles that mark multi-line scopes with showInSymbolList
(e.g. VHDL processes) turned into dozens of raw code fragments in the
symbol list. did_parse() now extends its range backward and forward
through adjacent symbol-marked scope runs and recomputes such symbols
whole, and the transformation is taken from the run that opens a symbol
rather than the last run before a break, so the preference that starts
a symbol also formats it.

The transformation parser also silently discarded every rule following
a separator written as ' ; ', which many bundles use; stray semicolons
between rules are now skipped.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
    076368014f Browse code
    Kazuhiro Sakai authored July 15, 2026

Jul 20, 2026

  1. Let .git-only changes reach scm clients … 

    Staging a file with `git add`, or committing work that was already
staged, leaves every tracked file byte-identical and every entry in the
status map unchanged. Both of the update path's short-circuits — the
working-tree snapshot comparison and the status-map equality check —
therefore held, and no client heard about it. The watcher already
recognises these events (it invalidates the diff blob cache on exactly
the same condition); it simply had no way to say "this mattered even
though nothing below .git moved".

Repo-meta changes now raise a flag that forces both the recompute and
the notification. The visible symptom was a review pane whose Staged
chip only appeared once some unrelated file happened to change, and a
HEAD-moved banner that depended on a commit incidentally touching the
working tree.

Jul 17, 2026

  1. Cap dirty paragraph widths at the pending wrap column … 

    With soft wrap on, shrinking the text viewport — window resize, or the
markdown-preview/diff pane opening or being drag-resized — left a
horizontal scrollbar behind: set_wrapping()/set_viewport_size() only
mark paragraphs dirty and the actual re-flow happens lazily in
paragraph_t::layout() when a row becomes visible, so update_row()
stored widths still computed from soft lines wrapped at the previous,
wider column. Off-screen paragraphs can stay in that state
indefinitely, keeping the layout's aggregated content width — and the
text view frame reflectDocumentSize/refresh_helper_t derive from it —
at the old wrap width.

Remember the pending wrap width in set_wrapping() and have width()
clamp to it while the paragraph is dirty; layout() drops the bound
once the soft lines are re-flowed and the real width is known.
Unwrapped rows are unaffected, so content that legitimately overflows
still gets its scroller.

Jul 16, 2026

  1. Don't abort when format-on-save's working directory is gone … 

    -[NSTask launch] raises NSInvalidArgumentException when the working
directory does not exist, and TextMate's NSExceptionHandler escalates
the raise to abort() before the surrounding @catch can run. A window's
projectPath is sticky (seeded from the first pathed document it shows)
and can outlive the directory it points to — observed as a hard crash
on save when a temporary directory that had seeded a scratch window's
project path was later deleted. Only set the task's cwd when the
directory actually exists.

byte-range edits suitable for -[OakDocument performReplacements:] (with

Mar 20, 2026

  1. Fix UI deadlock when bundle commands spawn processes that inherit pipes … 

    Decouple process exit from pipe drain in run_command. Previously, the
completion handler only fired when all dispatch group members finished
(waitpid + stdout reader + stderr reader). If a grandchild process like
mate inherited the pipe FDs, the readers would block forever, deadlocking
the main thread's modal event loop.

Now waitpid runs independently, then gives pipes a 500ms grace period to
drain before firing the completion handler regardless. Pipe readers
continue harmlessly in the background with no FD closing or data races.
    6b055349e0 Browse code

Dec 25, 2018

  1. Implement "Symbols" accessibility rotor … 

    Accessibility rotors allow VoiceOver user to navigate content quickly
by making possible navigation through select elements only.

In this case, we enable VoiceOver users to navigate efficiently
through symbols.

The first way to invoke a rotor is a "global" one (does not take into
account current position in text) and is invoked with VO-U. After
pressing arrow left/right sufficient times to reach "Symbols", one is
presented with a list analogical to the "Jump to symbols" TextMate
feature invokable by Shift-Cmd-T. Arrow up and down then enable
navigating through items, Return selects the result (and jumps to it),
Esc cancels the interface without moving the cursor. Also filtering
the list works by simply typing characters (implemented as
case-insensitive substring search - consistent e.g. with Safari's
"Headings" rotor).

The second way to use a rotor is a "local" one (navigates w.r.t. the
current position in text) and is typically done through Trackpad
Commander (turned on by VO + two finger "screw" gesture to the right
on the Trackpad). Then one uses two-finger "screw" gesture (like
(un)screwing the bottle lid from/to the bottle with thumb and index
finger) to select "Symbols". When this is finally selected (the
selection is persistent), the user can then use flick with one finger
up or down gestures to move to the previous/next occurrence respectively.

I made a choice at one spot - I report the "symbol location - end of
hardline" as the range of the symbol (that is e.g. what VoiceOver
reads when navigating the elements). This seemed to work best for the
user at least in the Objective-C code.

The APIs are 10.13+ only, so appropriate avaiability declarations are
put in place to not cause warnings from the compiler. I was not sure
whether some declaration like that is needed also for the
OakTextView's informal category's conformance to the
`NSAccessibilityCustomRotorItemSearchDelegate` protocol - the protocol
is 10.13+ only too, but the compiler does not warn about conforming to
it. Perhaps the Objective-C runtime is smart enough to take into
account that the `NSAccessibilityCustomRotorItemSearchDelegate` symbol
is (hopefully) weakly-linked and adds conformance to it (I assume
using the `class_addProtocol` function) only when it is non-nil. I
have however not tested whether the compiled app actually degrades
gracefully (without crashing) on macOS 10.12 and earlier, though (for
starters, I seem not to have access to a macOS Sierra image to create
a VM).
    85d3af94ba Browse code

old accessibility APIs are now deprecated. These APIs require a
minimum deployment target of 10.10, which is fulfilled since TextMate

typed, so it is no longer necessary to convert parameters from (and

Jul 20, 2016

  1. Use weak storage for GutterView's partnerView … 

    On 10.12 beta 3, when closing a window, the following exception is thrown:

Exception Name: NSInternalInconsistencyException
Description: <GutterView 0x7fa71c511150> has reached dealloc but still has a super view. Super views strongly reference there children, so this is being over-released, or has been over-released in the past.

Despite the mention of our GutterView instance being over-released, the actual problem is that we do not call super in our override of `removeFromSuperView`, where we nil out our partner view. A simple fix to avoid crashing would be just calling super in that method so that the view is marked as being removed; however, we can simplify the code and eliminate the need to override our super's method by using a weak reference instead and let ARC automatically handle the zeroing of our partner view.

May 31, 2016

  1. Exclude given scopes when extending selection … 

    This introduces new scope setting - excludeFromParagraphSelection, that
prevents extending selection to some scopes, eg. on comment.line.

Previously when reformatting paragraph comment lines were selected as paragraph
lines, this have led to mixing comment content into reformatted paragraph
content breaking the syntax of reformatted code, eg.:

  some very long ... line of text
  # some comment
  some other long ... line of text

As an effect we got:

  some very long ...
  ... text # some comment some other ...
  ... line of text

The problem described above was especially visible when using ⌃Q to Reformat
block of Git commit message, when below of the typed text there was a Git
default comment. Also this problem could be noticeable by authors using LaTeX.

This change checks whether a candidate line scope for paragraph extension has a
excludeFromParagraphSelection set to true and breaks upon such line, eg.
comment line.

Doing Select Paragraph ⌃⌥P again will select the comment as well.

Dec 28, 2015

  1. Use panel language unless spellingLanguage is specified … 

    This partially reverts changes of 3fdc72b93af0167e234c48314658d702f65a8a5f:
Support spell checking being “automatic by language”.

Before 3fdc72b spellingLanguage .tm_properties setting (default "en") was the
only way to set spelling language for file (buffer). English was default
language for all files. 3fdc72b introduced change that when “automatic by
language” was selected in system's spelling panel then TextMate was ignoring
spellingLanguage setting and was using automatic by language.

However because “automatic by language” is default on OS X, effectively 3fdc72b
makes spellingLanguage setting no longer effective. To make it work one needs
to set explicit spelling language either in System Preferences or in spelling
panel upon each TextMate run (since this is getting reset after application
restart) - which is counter-intuitive, can be treated as regression and it is
vaguely described in ChangeLog:

 * Support spell checking being “automatic by language”. This is set via the
   spelling panel.

This change presents alternative approach, introducing new empty
spellingLanguage setting "" (which is now default), which makes use system
panel language setting, including “automatic by language”.

From now on all files will be checked against system panel selected language
(or automatic), unless .tm_properties project specifies explicitly language for
given file using, eg.:

    [ locale-en_US.ini ]
    spellingLanguage = en_US

    [ locale-pl_PL.ini ]
    spellingLanguage = pl_PL

Or automatically depending on file name:

    [ locale-*.ini ]
    spellingLanguage = '${TM_FILEPATH/^.*locale-([a-z]+_[A-Z]+).*$/$1/}'

  1. Add support for commit and continue in the commit window … 

    The use case for this feature is when an interactive rebase is in
progress and be able to, in one command, amend the current commit
and continue with rebase.

By default, if the --rebase-in-progress flag is passed when the
"commit" command is invoked the commit button will be in a
"commit and continue" state. This is indicated by the title of the
commit button now being "Commit & Continue". If the option (⌥) key
is being hold down the state will revert back to the standard "commit"
state and the title will change to "Continue".

If the butten was clicked when it was in the "commit and continue"
state the "commit" command will print "TM_SCM_COMMIT_CONTINUE=1"
(without the quotes) to stdout as the last line. If the button was
clicked when it was in the standard "commit" state the output may
contain "TM_SCM_COMMIT_CONTINUE=0", or the "TM_SCM_COMMIT_CONTINUE"
string will be absent.

Nov 26, 2014

  1. Reorder accessibility order of chooser cell view items … 

    When VoiceOver users want to efficiently find an item in a list, they often go
through the items quickly, hearing just first few characters to decide whether
it is the item they want or whether it is positively not the one (in which case
they move to the next item). Therefore it is necessary for each row (item) of a
table to be worded in such a way for VoiceOver so that the most important piece
of information is read first, then followed by the less important piece of
information, etc.

E.g. for the file chooser, the most important piece of information about a file
is its file name. So we put that first for the VoiceOver user. If they are
unsure whether it is the right one (perhaps because there is more than one file
with the same name in different directories), then path to the file is read
after that.

Fixes textmate/bugs#10

  1. Do not use `convertBaseToScreen:` and `convertScreenToBase:` …

  2. Do not use `convertPointToBase:` and `convertPointFromBase:` … 

    These methods were deprecated in 10.7 and log warnings in the console when called. The documentation says to use `convertPointToBacking:` and `convertPointFromBacking:`, respectively, instead; however, these methods should not really be used in this case. We just want to store the top left position (point) of the OakChoiceMenu's frame in the OakDocumentView's coordinate systems so we can update its frame to the new position when OakDocumentView's bounds change. We do not need exact pixel alignment. The original choice to use the above deprecated methods was probably based on the use of `convertBaseToScreen:` and `convertScreenToBase:`, but these were also deprecated in 10.7. They can be replaced with the equivalent `convertRectToScreen:` and `convertRectFromScreen:`, respectively.

So instead, for this case, `convertRect:toView:` and `convertRect:fromView:` suffices and actually yields better tracking. (We could have used the corresponding "point" methods, as well, but we needed to convert the point to a NSRect to use `convertScreenFromRect:`, etc.)

With the original code, when the view bounds change, the position of the OakChoiceMenu would extend well below/above the placement of the caret.

Implementation of accessibilityAttributeValue:forParameter: returns nil for
some attributes. This is a hack to avoid doing tedious adjustments of certain
parameterized attributes (like AXStringForRange, AXAttributedStringForRange,
AXBoundsForRange, AXRTFForRange) for string AXValue that is extended (appended)
by extra information at its end in accessibilityAttributeValue:. To get an idea
how tedious this is (even though our case is a bit simpler by not *prepending*
anything before the AXValue, and not being an editable field), look at
OakLinkedSearchFieldCell. This looses the ability for the user to interact with
the text, but considering how seldom this will be used (if at all), for now
this seems acceptable.

This is needed because VoiceOver asks for the *StringForRange attributes and if
implemented, will never query AXValue (which is where our custom behavior is).

In the future when tables will be migrated from cell-based to view-based ones,
the tab trigger or shortcut could be a separate NSView, which would probably
allow for much more elegant solution to this problem.

Jun 22, 2014

  1. Use NSAccessibilitySharedFocusElementsAttribute in OakChooser … 

    This new 10.10 API allows one to mark, for some UI element, a set of UI
elements to track selection. VoiceOver (and other accessibility clients)
will then track and announce selection (cursor) changes not only in the
currently focused element, but also for all elements contained in its
"shared focus elements" array. This is a perfect fit for search field
with a table of results. In fact it is used for new 10.10 Spotlight -
its search field's shared focus element is the table containing the results.

As NSAccessibilitySharedFocusElementsAttribute is available only in the 10.10 SDK,
so make a way to use its value with previous SDKs (with which TextMate
is currently compiled).

We also retain the kind-of-hacky solution for pre-10.10 OSes introduced in
and instead use NSAccessibilitySharedFocusElementsAttribute.

This code was tested in all 6 fields of a 3×2 matrix:
* compiled with 10.8, 10.9 and 10.10 SDK
* run on 10.9 and 10.10 (DP2)

For user, this means more standard behavior (says the same "completion selected"
thing as with Spotlight) and a bit more correctness (no extra space
before beginning / after end of search field on braille display).

For developer, this means once we stop supporting 10.9, we will be ready to
drop a lot of code which, while serving us well to make the choosers more
user friendly on pre-10.10, will no longer be needed.

Mar 8, 2014

  1. Workaround for accessibility of OakChooser's search field … 

    Currently for VoiceOver user when the text cursor is at the end of the search
field (which is 99% of the time) and the user wants to navigate the results
in the table view using arrow down, then after each arrow down, VoiceOver first
plays a "end-of-text" sound, then announces whole contents of the search field,
and only then announces the newly selected search result. (The same happens
when text cursor is at the beginning of the search field and user presses
arrow up.)

This is probably a bug in the way AppKit handles text field accessibility - see
http://lists.apple.com/archives/accessibility-dev/2014/Feb/msg00019.html

I also reported this as <rdar://problem/16271507>

I hereby present a hacky workaround for this - a subclass of NSSearchField
that tricks accessibility into thinking there is one extra space before and
after the text in the search field. Therefore VoiceOver will not think the user
is at the end of text when they actually are, and therefore will not play the
"end-of-text" sound and announce whole contents of the search field before
getting to the information user wants (the newly selected search result).

While this is a bit hacky, along with the previous commit it allows VoiceOver
to have the same instant great experience as a sighted user when filtering
and browsing results in OakChooser. So I think it's worth the hackiness until
there is a better alternative.

There is only last issue, as currently VoiceOver is very chatty when the
OakChooser window appears: first says "Go to file", if user interrupts it with
an action (i.e. moving VO cursor or typing a character), then VoiceOver starts
telling the whole title of the window, and only after user interrupts it again
does VoiceOver say or announce only the user actions (including search results
table selection change).

So the simpliest if the user wants to start navigating the table items
immediately after showing the OakChooser's window (i.e. without entering
a search term) is to, after showing the OakChooser (e.g. with ⌘T or ⇧⌘T),
quickly type any letter and immediately delete it with backspace and then
use arrow down/up.
    129cc2749d Browse code
    Boris Dušek authored March 8, 2014

  2. Announce current OakChooser item to accessibility … 

    This solves accessibility of situation of a user browsing results in
OakChooser (currently File Chooser and Symbol Chooser). Typically
the user is in search field and after typing the search string
wants to use arrow down and up to browse results.

The problem this presented to accessibility was that VoiceOver reads
only changes of selection in the current VoiceOver item. As the user
is on the search field but the selection changes in the results table
below, VoiceOver did not read the various search results when pressing
arrow up/down.

Alternative was to leave the search field, move to the results table,
interact with it and then navigate it with VoiceOver. This is however
not the desired user experience comparable to that of sighted users,
as the VoiceOver user still has to do quite a few steps after entering
the search string to browse the results, not to speak about the situation
when the user would like to change the search string - he/she would need
to leave the table and get back to the search field.

This solves the problem by making the search field (or more generally
any user interface element that triggers change of selection in the
results table, which should be the element the VoiceOver cursor is on)
announce to accessibility the contents of the selected row in search
results table.

See this thread on accessibility-dev mailing list where the options for
implementing such a user interface in an accessible way are discussed:

http://lists.apple.com/archives/accessibility-dev/2013/Dec/msg00000.html
and
http://lists.apple.com/archives/accessibility-dev/2014/Feb/msg00016.html

If the user did not move selection (it is on the first line) and they
want to hear it, they should use arrow up to hear it. Then they can
use arrow down to move through results.

    Boris Dušek authored March 8, 2014

  3. Use softlines instead of hardlines for accessibility … 

    Fixes #1149.

VoiceOver expects AXLineForIndex and AXRangeForLine to be consistent with
the movement by line using arrow up/down. That means it expects "line"
to mean softline.

VoiceOver also distinguishes commands to move by:
* paragraph (hardline): VO-Shift-PgUp/PgDown
* line (softline): VO-up/down

These are available when interacting with the text area (VO-Shift-down).

This commit therefore fixes the AXLineForIndex and AXRangeForLine
to make "line" mean "softline" instead of "hardline" as was the case
until now.

Sep 8, 2013

  1. Support text attributes with VoiceOver … 

    VoiceOver can announce text formatting, such as bold font, italics,
underline, font, etc., as well as whether text is misspelled. For this,
it needs the AXAttributedStringForRange attribute supported. This commit
does exactly that.

Testing can be done in this way (VO stands for Ctrl-Option):

* first interact with the text (VO-Shift-down arrow when standing
  on the text element)
* to announce text attributes for character after cursor, press VO-T
* to seek for next:
  * misspelled text: VO-Cmd-E
  * color change:    VO-Cmd-K
  * underlined text: VO-Cmd-U
  * many more (see VO-H-H, "Find", close help with Esc)
* to seek for previous *: just add Shift to the shortcut

Some attributes remain to be supported (full list of attributes is available at: https://developer.apple.com/library/mac/documentation/cocoa/reference/applicationkit/Protocols/NSAccessibility_Protocol/Reference/Reference.html#//apple_ref/doc/uid/20000945-SW53).

The misspelled text VoiceOver support can be used nicely with TextMate's
spelling support:

1. the user finds next mistake with VO-Cmd-E, hears the misspelled word,
   perhaps reads it on a braille display
2. the user then presses Cmd-; to show the spelling menu for that word
   and chooses the desired resolution (apply suggested correction etc.)
3. go back to step 1. :-)

  2. Present the document view as a group to VoiceOver/accessibility … 

    This enables VoiceOver user to see the document view as a single
element and interact with it (i.e. inspect its subelements) only when
needed by using the VO-Shift-down shortcut (and stop interacting with
it using VO-Shift-up shortcut). This makes the element structure more
hierarchical where at the top level are only major user interface
components, so that it's easier for orientation. It also prevents
unrelated UI elements to be sequential as VoiceOver by default orders
elements by the visual order (top-down, left-right) rather then
the order in the AXChildren array. For example in this case,
the bottom status bar of the document window gets separated from
the bottom toolbar of the file browser, unlike the situation before
grouping when both bars were adjacent to the VoiceOver user.
    f4e2de14f2 Browse code
    Boris Dušek authored March 2, 2013

  3. Make macro recording an NSToggleButton … 

    This fixes semantics of the button and thus also its
accessibility. The macro recording button represents state - more
specifically a boolean state, so it has to be a NSToggleButton (or
its specialization). Then the button is presented to the VoiceOver
user as an AXCheckbox - that is a checkbox with on and off value -
which is exactly what the button's function is. Examples of this in
system apps is e.g. the "Play" button in QuickTime Player, which is
also an AXCheckbox ("Pause" is then simply an unchecked "Play"
checkbox).
    944e1e32fa Browse code
    Boris Dušek authored March 2, 2013

  4. Fix initial accessibility of symbol pop-up … 

    VoiceOver reads an AXValue for a pop-up button - that is the selected
item. But button's title does not set an AXValue, as it probably is
not a menu item. So change the code set to the title by setting a
single menu item with that title.

This fixes accessibility of the pop-up when accessing its value before
it is first popped up. It makes the code consistent with setGrammarName:
which works fine (that's how I discovered how to fix it).
